1.title: Know online learning
1.intro: Online education means teaching and learning through the internet. Learn the main forms and the words.
pts: Name the forms: live class, recorded lessons, self-paced course, coaching, community group.
Describe the parts of a course: goal, lessons, practice, feedback, check.
Explain the difference between live and self-paced learning.
List words: outcome, module, assessment, rubric, learner.
1.ex: A short course on basic budgeting has 4 recorded lessons, 4 practice tasks and a live question hour each week.
1.act: Take one free short online lesson. Write what helped you learn and what did not.
1.std: Task: name parts of an online course. Condition: from one real lesson. Standard: five parts named with one example each.

2.title: Know your learner
2.intro: Good teaching starts with knowing who will learn, what they know and what they need.
pts: Describe your learner: age, work, language, devices, time, internet access.
Ask three learners what they want to do after the course.
Check for barriers: cost, time zone, disability, low bandwidth, language.
Explain why plain words and clear steps help every learner.
2.ex: Learners are shift workers with phones and weak internet. The course uses short lessons, text and low-size audio, with a printable page.
2.act: Interview three possible learners and write a one-page learner profile.
2.std: Task: write a learner profile. Condition: three interviews. Standard: needs, barriers and goals written with real quotes.

3.title: Follow the rules in Canada
3.intro: Education, consumer, privacy and copyright rules apply. Check with the local authority.
pts: Explain that education is a provincial matter; some private training must be registered or approved; check your province.
Describe consumer protection for course fees, refunds and honest claims.
Apply privacy rules for learner data and, for minors, extra care and parent consent.
Check copyright: use your own work or material you have permission or a licence to use.
3.ex: Rules table row: Private training approval | provincial education body | check if your course type needs registration | before selling | written reply kept.
3.act: Make a rules table covering approval, consumer rules, privacy and copyright for your province.
3.std: Task: map the rules. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a checked date.

4.title: Design a course with clear outcomes
4.intro: Start with what learners will be able to do, then build lessons and checks to match.
pts: Write 4 to 6 outcomes with action verbs such as explain, apply, build, check.
Build a course map: outcome, lesson, practice, check.
Apply the rule: one main idea per lesson and one task per idea.
Compare your plan with a real task a learner will do after the course.
4.ex: Outcome: apply a monthly budget. Lesson: income and costs. Practice: fill a sheet from a sample case. Check: a short quiz and a review of the sheet.
4.act: Build a course map for a topic you know and ask two people to find gaps.
4.std: Task: design a course map. Condition: one topic. Standard: every outcome has a lesson, a practice and a check.

5.title: Make clear lessons and tools
5.intro: Short, clear lessons beat long ones. Use simple tools you can manage.
pts: Build a lesson: aim, short explanation, example, task, feedback.
Apply plain words, short sentences and one picture per idea.
Check accessibility: captions or text, readable colours, keyboard use, low data.
Choose simple tools for video, documents and quizzes; test on a phone.
5.ex: A five-minute lesson: one aim, a two-minute explanation, one worked example, a task and a model answer shown after the learner tries.
5.act: Build one lesson with a task and test it with three learners on their own devices.
5.std: Task: build a lesson. Condition: for a phone. Standard: three learners complete the task and say what the aim was.

6.title: Teach, give feedback and check learning
6.intro: People learn by doing and by feedback. Checking must match the outcome.
pts: Apply feedback: say what worked, what to change, and the next step.
Build a simple rubric with three levels for each task.
Evaluate checks: do they test the outcome or only memory?
Explain academic honesty and how to handle copied work.
6.ex: Rubric row: Budget sheet | Not yet: totals wrong | Meets: totals right | Strong: totals right and a plan to cut one cost.
6.act: Mark three practice submissions with your rubric and write feedback for each.
6.std: Task: give feedback. Condition: three submissions. Standard: each feedback names a strength, a change and a next step.

7.title: Price, sell and support
7.intro: Learners pay for results and trust. Price fairly and be clear about what is included.
pts: Compute cost per learner: time, tools, support, payment fees, tax.
Compare pricing: one fee, monthly fee, free with paid support.
Write honest claims about results; never promise jobs or income.
Track the funnel: visitors, sign-ups, starters, finishers.
7.ex: Price 65 per hour of live help, direct cost 0. If fixed costs are 500 a month, break-even is about 8 hours. Completion rate 60% means the first two lessons need work.
7.act: Build a cost sheet and a one-page offer, and invite 20 people to a free first lesson.
7.std: Task: price a course. Condition: all costs counted. Standard: break-even correct and the offer makes no unsupported promises.

8.title: Run the course for real
8.intro: Now run your course with real learners, measure results and improve it.
pts: Run a 60-day pilot with a stop rule agreed in advance.
Review weekly: sign-ups, completion, feedback, task results.
Create a 12-month plan: updates, new courses and support.
Lead others: train a helper to answer questions and mark tasks with your rubric.
8.ex: Stop rule: if fewer than 10 learners finish in 60 days, rebuild the first two lessons. Result: 14 finished; learners ask for a second course.
8.act: Run the pilot, write the review and present your plan to three people.
8.std: Task: run an online course pilot. Condition: 60 days, real learners. Standard: results compared with the stop rule and rules re-checked with the provincial body.

quiz: Name the parts of a course.
Goal, lessons, practice, feedback and check.
Why write a learner profile?
To design for real needs, barriers and goals.
Who sets education rules in Canada?
The provinces; check yours.
Why start with outcomes?
They decide what lessons, practice and checks you need.
Which verbs fit an outcome?
Action verbs such as explain, apply, build, check.
What makes a lesson accessible?
Captions or text, readable colours, keyboard use and low data size.
What is a rubric?
A table of levels that shows how work is judged.
What should good feedback include?
A strength, a change and a next step.
Why avoid promises of jobs or income?
Claims must be honest and you cannot control the outcome.
What do you do about copyright?
Use your own work or material you have permission or licence for.
